---
title: "Study 06 — kpush should scale with size"
subtitle: "Why the same bias is gentler on a bigger cluster — the per-atom normalization"
---

## The law

xTB's bias is a Gaussian in **root-mean-square** deviation,
$V = k_\text{push}\,e^{-\alpha\,\mathrm{RMSD}^2}$ with
$\mathrm{RMSD}^2 = \frac1N\sum_i|x_i-x_i^\text{ref}|^2$. The bias force on an atom,

$$F_i = k_\text{push}\,\alpha\,e^{-\alpha\,\mathrm{RMSD}^2}\,\frac{2}{N}\,(x_i-x_i^\text{ref}),$$

carries an explicit **1/N** — the same `kpush` pushes each atom $1/N$ as hard in a
bigger system. To keep the per-atom bias effect constant, **`kpush` must scale
∝ N** (per-atom; per-molecule is the same with $N=3\times\#\text{waters}$).

![Fixed `kpush` follows the 1/N line (diluted); N-scaled `kpush` holds the
per-atom force constant across n=3→96 atoms.](assets/kpush_scaling_law.png){width=520}

## Empirical confirmation

The trimer first fragments at `kpush = 0.008`, so the N-scaling predicts the
30-water droplet reaches the same per-atom bias at
`kpush ≈ 0.008 × 90/9 = 0.08`. The droplet is intact up to 0.05 — and at ~0.08 it
starts shedding a molecule, right on the prediction.

![Intact through kpush 0.05; onset of fragmentation at the N-scaled
~0.08.](assets/kpush_confirmation_n30.png){width=520}

::: {.callout-note}
## Caveat
The onset is soft because size changes two things at once: it dilutes the
per-atom force (1/N — corrected here) **and** raises cohesion (more H-bonds per
interior molecule). The `kpush ∝ N` law fixes the first exactly; the second means
a big droplet still resists a bit more than bare force-scaling predicts.
:::

**Practical rule:** set `kpush` per atom, `kpush_eff = kpush_ref · N / N_ref`, so
bias strength is comparable across cluster sizes.
